note.specFocus: Christian teaching on sexual relationships, and the range of Christian attitudes to same-sex relationships.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.4 Human Relationships
Christian teaching generally links sexual relationships closely to marriage, though attitudes to specific relationships vary between denominations.
Heterosexual relationships
• Genesis 2:24 describes marriage as the context in which "a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh" — many Christians see marriage as the intended setting for sexual intimacy.
• Sex within marriage is traditionally understood to serve both unity (strengthening the couple's bond) and procreation (having children), though views on strictness around sex outside marriage vary between conservative and more liberal Christians.
Same-sex relationships
• Traditionalist Christians cite passages such as Leviticus 18:22 and Romans 1:26–27 as evidence that the Bible condemns same-sex sexual acts, and so teach that marriage should remain between a man and a woman.
• More inclusive Christian traditions (e.g. Quakers, the United Reformed Church, and parts of the Anglican Communion) emphasise Jesus' teaching to love one's neighbour and the equal worth of all people made in God's image, and have moved towards blessing or permitting same-sex marriages.
• Differences often come down to how each tradition interprets the Bible: whether certain Old Testament laws are seen as timeless commands or as culturally bound and no longer directly binding.
Exam link: when discussing "different attitudes", name specific denominations or traditions (e.g. Catholic vs Quaker) rather than generalising about "some Christians" without any detail.

evidence: Marriage as the context for sex
questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Most Christians teach that marriage between a man and a woman is the proper context for a sexual relationship, based on Genesis 2:24, "a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh".

2. Christians generally see heterosexual relationships within marriage as intended by God for both the expression of love and unity between partners and, traditionally, for having and raising children, though views on strictness vary between denominations.

evidence: Inclusive church traditions (e.g. Quakers, some Anglicans)
Biblical interpretation and the Great Commandment
questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Some Christians, often described as traditionalist or conservative, cite passages such as Leviticus 18:22 and Romans 1:26–27 as evidence that same-sex sexual relationships are condemned in scripture, and so teach that homosexual relationships are against God's design for marriage.

Second, Other, more inclusive Christians, including many within the Anglican, United Reformed and Quaker traditions, emphasise Jesus' teaching to love one's neighbour and the equal worth of all people made in God's image, arguing that loving, committed same-sex relationships can be blessed by God.

Finally, Differences also arise because denominations interpret the Bible differently: some read certain Old Testament laws as no longer binding on Christians, while others treat them as timeless moral commands, which is why there is no single Christian position and why views continue to change over time.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of agape, faithfulness, marriage, cohabitation and diversity of Christian teaching and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
